#43544. ConceptARC at Scale: Studying Conceptual Understanding in Reasoning Models

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (252 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

ConceptARC at Scale: Studying Conceptual Understanding in Reasoning Models

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (252 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

In a recent development, arXiv:2611.06732v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large reasoning models (LRMs) perform well on challenging benchmarks, yet it remains unclear whether they form generalizable abstractions across conceptually related reasoning tasks. The Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus (ARC) provides a controlled testbed for studying abstraction, requiring solvers to infer transformation rules over two-dimensional grids from a small set of examples. While ARC evaluates rule abstraction within individual tasks, different tasks may share higher-level structure despite requiring different transformations$\unicode{x2014}$for example, several tasks may involve reasoning about objects contained within other objects. Benchmarks such as ConceptARC capture this structure by grouping ARC-style tasks into recurring spatial and semantic concepts, but they often contain only a few manually constructed tasks per concept. We introduce ConceptARC at Scale, a generator for creating thousands of ARC-style tasks targeting a specific concept. Using this generator, we construct ConceptARC-100, a dataset of 1,600 new, manually reviewed tasks, with 100 tasks for each of the 16 concepts defined by ConceptARC$\unicode{x2014}$ten times the size of the original benchmark. We evaluate a range of recent LRMs and models trained from scratch on ConceptARC-100 to characterize which concepts they solve reliably and where they struggle. We further analyze the models' internal representations and find clear semantic structure: task representations cluster according to the operations applied to objects, such as recoloring, removal, or translation, even when realized through substantially different rules and scenarios. Together, our results suggest that models form stable abstractions of transformation operations that generalize across diverse tasks.

AceAction-5M: Hierarchical Goals for Generalist Action Learning Across 3D Game Worlds

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (194 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.04241v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Video games provide a practical setting for collecting vision-language-action (VLA) data, whose acquisition in physical environments is costly. Existing datasets, however, remain limited by restricted game coverage, sparse language supervision, or temporal hierarchies that do not necessarily reflect changes in task objectives. We introduce AceAction, a dataset of human gameplay across multiple 3D games for learning skill composition and subgoal transitions. AceAction organizes demonstrations around complete tasks, linking overall instructions, ordered subgoals, and local skill instructions to temporally aligned visual observations and keyboard-and-mouse actions. To construct these annotations, we develop a vision-language model pipeline that identifies subgoals from changes in objectives or interaction targets, anchors navigation goals to visually recognizable waypoints, and composes adjacent subgoals into task instructions. The resulting demonstrations cover navigation, reconnaissance, combat, interaction, and recovery, with explicit stage boundaries that connect task progression to fine-grained control. We assess annotation quality through model-based verification and human inspection. An audit of 500 trajectories yields a 95.8% pass rate across independent reviewer assessments. AceAction provides a data foundation for studying how agents execute, combine, and switch skills to follow complex instructions in dynamic game environments.

Tech Report: Researcher-in-the-Loop Evolutionary Discovery of Entanglement-Assisted Quantum Code Families

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (207 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2610.41183v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: LLM-guided program evolution can produce mathematical constructions, but validity, generality, and reproducibility require distinct evidence. In this paper, we develop a researcher-in-the-loop discovery pipeline combining program evolution, exact evaluation, mathematical generalization, and independent verification. We apply it to entanglement-assisted quantum error-correcting codes (EAQECCs). Evolved programs produced finite qubit constructions from specifications that supplied no family formula. Researcher-directed analysis with a language model led to a general construction and proof drafts, which the researchers revised and checked. The resulting family $[[n,1,n-1;n-q-1]]_q$ exists for prime powers $q\ge3$ at $n\ge2q+1$ and for $q=2$ at odd $n\ge5$; Lean checks its formalized algebraic core. With entanglement lifting, it closes 54 listed table gaps. The evidence includes 115 verified code records, ten DRAT-checked nonexistence results, family implementations and preserved search programs. Controlled studies test how research proposals interact with program generation. Under a mutation-and-restart proposal, iterative evolution improves normalized success-curve area in all ten paired runs and raises success at excluded lengths $n=13,15$ from 13.4% to 62.5% and from 0.9% to 33.4%, respectively. The benefit depends on the proposal. Selected programs combine the proposed moves with objective and restart-counter changes. The pipeline connects finite computational discoveries to a proved family and independently checkable constructions.

Kairos: Fast and Reliable Symbolic Task Planning for Autonomous Robots

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (257 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2610.39454v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Robots that plan while they act need a task planner that reads the models their designers write, answers within milliseconds, and says what each answer means. Models are written in the Planning Domain Definition Language (PDDL), which has grown from classical planning to durative actions, numeric resources, time windows and continuous change, while planners cover one fragment each and differ in what their failures mean. The contribution in artificial intelligence is Kairos, a single planner, not a portfolio of existing planners, that covers the whole language and derives what each answer guarantees from the search that produced it. We prove when the exhaustion of a search reveals that no plan exists, and give a relaxation of temporal tasks that proves unsolvability where temporal search cannot. For the compression of durative actions, we give a criterion on the values that actions read, prove that compression is sound, and show that it is not complete, so its failure is never reported as a proof. An independent validator checks every plan. The engineering application is on-line task planning for robots: Kairos is open source, packaged for the Robot Operating System, and the default planner of a widely used planning framework. On 1,756 public tasks from nine suites, Kairos solves more tasks than the strongest evaluated planner of each suite within 100 milliseconds, 1 second and 30 seconds; it proves ten of eleven unsolvable tasks, and handles each of the seventeen language features probed, where no other planner handles more than eight.

Heimstaden is changing residential real estate management with AI

💡 Key Takeaways
  • From rethinking how homes are rented out to building AI-powered property operations, Heimstaden is using OpenAI to improve how it manages homes.
  • It has been revealed that A hundred years ago, managing a residential building meant finding tenants, collecting rent and keeping properties in good condition.
  • For European residential real estate operator Heimstaden⁠(opens in a new window), this presents an opportunity: what if AI could fundamentally change how thousands of homes are managed?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

From rethinking how homes are rented out to building AI-powered property operations, Heimstaden is using OpenAI to improve how it manages homes.

Reduction in property image production costs.

Property assets analyzed with Codex.

Employee adoption within 2-3 months.

It has been revealed that A hundred years ago, managing a residential building meant finding tenants, collecting rent and keeping properties in good condition. Today, these fundamentals remain remarkably similar. What is changing is how that work gets done.

For European residential real estate operator Heimstaden⁠(opens in a new window), this presents an opportunity: what if AI could fundamentally change how thousands of homes are managed?

In June 2025, Heimstaden’s leadership decided to accelerate its bet on AI. After evaluating several platforms, the company chose OpenAI. The goal was twofold; empower employees and rethink the processes at the heart of its business.

The ambition is to move towards increasingly self-operating buildings, where AI can help anticipate needs, coordinate work and support decisions across the property lifecycle. “The purpose of our buildings hasn’t changed.” indicates Helge Krogsbøl, Co-CEO at Heimstaden. “We provide homes for people. But the way we operate them continues to change as we challenge conventions and adopt new technology.”.

“We see AI as one of the biggest opportunities to accelerate that transformation.”.

Consider what happens when a property becomes vacant.

Traditionally, getting it back onto the market involves assessing rental value, arranging photography, producing advertisements and responding to market demand. Each stage requires time, coordination and specialist input. And it is an information challenge; understanding what you own, what the competition has, and what the customer wants.

AI is now supporting all the key steps in this process:.

Pricing: Intelligence and recommendations based on tools built in ChatGPT Sites.

Advertising: Image styling and apartment descriptions done by AI.

Review listings: Agent reviews all live ads against Heimstaden’s quality standards.

Feedback: AI generated market feedback helps letting teams take corrective action which makes prices increasingly dynamic.

Employees remain responsible for reviewing and approving decisions. But the work surrounding those decisions is changing.

It has been revealed that in the Netherlands, the cost of producing a virtually staged property image has fallen from approximately €50 to less than €0.10 which is a reduction of more than 99%. Heimstaden estimates annual savings potential of €130,000 in that market alone.

Industry observers note that the significance extends beyond cheaper advertisements. By applying AI across the letting process, Heimstaden is building a more responsive way to bring homes to market.

Recent findings suggest that “Our AI strategy is based on three pillars.” claims Nikolaj Brammer, Heimstaden’s Chief Digital Officer, “First, we empower employees through training and access to the right tools. Second, we have a central transformation office and a network of AI champions to drive larger AI initiatives. Third, we strengthen the foundations by making our property management systems and data models ready for AI.”.

Letting puts all three pillars into practice: tools and training enable colleagues to create virtually staged images and listings; our central team coordinates improvements across pricing, advertising, ad review and market feedback; and we are making property data accessible to the AI tools that support pricing and listing creation.

“We started by breaking down our most important business processes and asking where AI could create value. Letting is a good example: it’s not about automating one task, but improving how the whole process works.”.

Some of the most significant changes are happening far from traditional software engineering teams.

Heimstaden needed to assess environmental risks across its portfolio. The information existed, but was scattered across public sources, formats and datasets. Turning it into a usable assessment would have required substantial manual work and technical resources.

Heimstaden’s Julia Erlandsen, an environmental sustainability analyst without a software development background, used Codex to help build a different approach.

Industry observers note that codex supported the discovery, cleaning and standardisation of data, quality checking and the development of repeatable processing pipelines. Julia retained control over the methodology and validation.

The result: 20,112 assets assessed, more than six million rows of useful data generated, and an estimated delivery requirement reduced from five people working for a year to two people working for two months.

Heimstaden also avoided engaging external consultants which would otherwise have been needed to solve the problem.

What began as a complex analytical project is becoming a repeatable capability, supporting climate-risk assessments, reporting requirements and investor decision-making.

Industry observers note that “Codex helped us build a solution that would previously have required substantial technical support. We now own the methodology and can continue developing it ourselves.”.

Heimstaden’s AI adoption focuses on tasks employees need help with. After ChatGPT Enterprise debuted in September 2025, half of employees were using it within two to three months. A central AI transformation office maintains a library of use cases so colleagues can learn from examples across the business.

It has been revealed that employees use approved tools within rules for data security. They remain responsible for reviewing AI-generated content before sending it and for approving decisions.

In a recent development, adoption extends to real estate caretakers, including some who were initially sceptical. In Norway, one caretaker used ChatGPT to assess a neglected apartment and draft a prioritised refurbishment proposal, turning observations into a structured plan they could review and refine.

Industry observers note that “People across the business are finding practical ways to use AI in their daily work. Our job is to scale what works while keeping data secure, responsibilities clear and people in control.”.

Heimstaden is already preparing for the next stage: AI that can work across systems and coordinate multi-step processes.

Its Procurement Intelligence Platform, right now being rolled out, combines workflow automation with OpenAI models accessed through APIs. Designed to operate across Outlook, SharePoint and Teams, it supports contract analysis, negotiation preparation and contract lifecycle management, with employees retaining responsibility for commercial decisions and approvals.

The longer-term ambition is more fundamental.

Heimstaden is co-developing Amplio Estate, a modern property management system designed to support AI-powered workflows through MCP. The goal is to enable employees to use AI, such as ChatGPT, to retrieve property information and take action in core business systems, with appropriate human oversight.

This is how Heimstaden begins turning the idea of self-operating buildings into a practical technology roadmap.

More than 99% lower image production costs in the Netherlands.

20,112 property assets assessed with Codex, reducing the estimated delivery requirement from five people over one year to two people over two months.

50% employee adoption within 2–3 months of rollout.

Focus on people: Adoption and imagination are the bottlenecks (not tech).

Find your champions: The biggest returns come from colleagues driving change locally.

Get the process right: AI will not fix a broken process, but it can dramatically scale a good one.

Heimstaden’s vision is not of buildings without people, but of properties supported by increasingly intelligent systems which will improve decision making for employees and increase ability to resolve matters for customers.

The buildings will remain much as they have always been—homes and roofs over people’s heads. The way they’re operated has forever changed.

Latest Update: OwlSight: A Panoramic Monitor for Chain-of-Thought Reasoning

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (206 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

Recent findings suggest that arXiv:2610.23670v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) monitoring offers actionable evidence for oversight AI systems, with the potential to enable early detection and intervention. However, existing approaches are focused on specific tasks, whereas the regulation of AI, particularly reasoning models, requires monitoring a broader range of tasks. We introduce Factor for CoT monitoring, a strategy that supports customizing monitoring requirements in the prompt, which enables a single monitor to cover different tasks by relying on different factors. Furthermore, we introduce two types of factors, fine-grained and coarse-grained (e.g., monitoring whether a specific email address has been leaked versus monitoring privacy leakage), to accommodate diverse user monitoring needs. Based on this, we develop a CoT monitor named OwlSight that relies solely on factor to monitor behaviors related to multiple dimensions, including capability, safety, and trustworthiness. Experiments across 15,971 reasoning trajectories show that OwlSight surpasses general-purpose LLMs by 1.32-30.57 and 11.71-27.81 points at fine and coarse granularity, respectively, and achieves state-of-the-art results on OpenAI's CoT monitorability benchmark. It also generalizes to unseen models' CoTs and remains robust to Factor rephrasings, CoT compression, and obfuscation, offering a promising paradigm for CoT monitoring that can contribute to the oversight of frontier AI.

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

RAN-JEPA: An Action-Conditioned World Model for Energy-efficient Mobile Network Control

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (220 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

Sources indicate that arXiv:2610.17584v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Operational mobile networks are rich in observations but poor in interventions: they continuously generate large volumes of passive telemetry, while controlled action--response trajectories remain comparatively scarce and costly to collect. This observation--intervention asymmetry is a central obstacle to building practical world models for RAN control. We address this problem with RAN-JEPA, an action-conditioned world model that separates representation learning from intervention learning. The model first learns a predictive latent representation from observation-only network data, adapts that representation to the target deployment domain, and then learns action-conditioned latent dynamics from controlled sleep/wake trajectories while keeping the encoder fixed. We evaluate RAN-JEPA using public operator performance data for pretraining and a real-equipment four-cell 5G testbed for domain adaptation, post-training, and control. Across four future 15-minute intervals, RAN-JEPA achieves lower action-conditioned prediction error than a GPT-2 world-model baseline and a mechanistic rule, while remaining close to a strong persistence reference. What-if evaluation further highlights that the model produces distinct and coherent future trajectories under matched SLEEP and KEEP looks. In closed-loop control, RAN-JEPA consistently supports higher sleep ratios than the two baselines at comparable congestion cost. These results show that observation-first, action-conditioned learning can turn abundant passive telemetry and limited intervention data into a practical predictive model for energy-aware RAN control.

Where Can a Decision Model Diagnose HVAC Faults? Reasoning Demand, Physical Representation, and Robustness Under Shift

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (261 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

In a recent development, arXiv:2610.09937v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Artificial intelligence supports building operations in several forms, each with its own barrier. Expert rules must be tuned for every system, supervised models need labeled data that buildings rarely record, and language models return free text that requires human-in-the-loop checking, since their stated confidence is unreliable. A newer kind of pretrained model, here called a decision model, returns a probability for every allowed answer, so one model could serve many decisions without training. This study answers three open questions for fault diagnosis in heating, ventilation, and air-conditioning systems: which decisions such a model can make, what input it needs, and whether its probabilities hold when conditions change. On 128 fault days from four public datasets of real equipment, faults are graded by the reasoning their diagnosis demands, with data given raw, as physical features, or with Brick topology. The decision model Jev, open language models, and a supervised model face nine tests that change season, control configuration, or building. Given physical features, Jev and the larger open model diagnosed faults whose evidence one feature carries, but not faults that need operating context. Under shift they kept their accuracy and calibration, while the supervised model lost 0.33 macro-F1 yet led or tied within a building. Their probabilities still needed correction, and detection was weak. The study maps which faults a decision model can diagnose and from what input, and supports a division of work in which code computes the physics and the model ranks candidate faults for an operator.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Industry observers note that cisco builds the networking and security infrastructure that organizations rely on to connect and protect their systems.
  • It has been revealed that cisco’s defense starts where threats move: the network.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Cisco combines network intelligence and OpenAI models to build more adaptive defenses.

Industry observers note that cisco builds the networking and security infrastructure that organizations rely on to connect and protect their systems. As adversaries leverage AI to scale automated attacks and craft exploits at machine-speed, defending enterprise infrastructure must evolve. Pairing Cisco’s vast network telemetry with frontier AI reasoning gives defenders the toolkit necessary to outpace emerging threats. OpenAI’s rigorous approach to enterprise data privacy—centered on zero data retention, strict customer data boundaries, and verifiable isolation—means Cisco could confidently deploy frontier intelligence across mission-critical systems without compromising customer priorities or sensitive telemetry.

It has been revealed that cisco’s defense starts where threats move: the network. Patel describes a shift from a single security perimeter to controls distributed across microservices, containers, and clusters. “We can put a mini security stack in front of every microservice, every Kubernetes container, and every Kubernetes cluster, and fuse security into the fabric of the network,” he indicates.

Sources indicate that controls at the application level can restrict communication to the connections each service needs, reducing the paths an attacker can use to spread. Security teams can also isolate affected systems more selectively, allowing unaffected services to keep running while they investigate and respond.

Combining that network intelligence with OpenAI’s models allows Cisco to correlate signals at machine scale, Patel states. “Two signals might seem benign in isolation, but together they can reveal a meaningful pattern. Network intelligence allows us to correlate data across the network and derive insights to inform secure operations.”.

It has been revealed that patel points to a pressing challenge for defenders: the gap between how quickly attackers can exploit a vulnerability and how long organizations take to patch it. He sees AI as a way to help narrow that gap, giving defenders the capacity to investigate more threats and respond faster. “AI hands attackers speed and scale. Using AI for defense is a prerequisite for staying safe,” he states.

He describes initiatives like Daybreak and GPT‑6 Astra as advances that strengthen security for both Cisco and its customers. “We’re able to find and patch vulnerabilities more efficiently, while shortening the time needed for investigation, response, and remediation,” Patel says.

Patel sees a path to adoption that builds on the processes teams already use to find and address vulnerabilities. “These capabilities can fit into your existing scanning workflows, so you don’t have to fundamentally change how your team works.”.

As agents become more autonomous, security teams also need to distinguish malicious interference from an agent pursuing a legitimate goal in an unintended way. Patel says that requires security telemetry alongside observability data, so teams can assess both threats and agent behavior.

He outlines three priorities: protect agents from malicious attacks, detect and intercept unintended behavior, and operate in near real time. These priorities are guiding the shift towards policies and controls that can adapt as agents act.

Through the Daybreak Defense Network, Cisco and OpenAI are exploring how to help security teams triage exposure faster and enforce the right controls in Cisco Cloud Control. For Patel, that can help shift the advantage back to defenders.

According to recent reports, arXiv:2610.09335v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Autonomous unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) object search involves a closed loop of perception, decision-making, and action under partial observability. Urban environments pose several challenges: large search areas and narrow egocentric views limit coverage, dense 3D geometry constrains safe motion, and open-world instructions require identifying a specific target among distractors. Many existing methods mitigate partial observability through explicit maps or memory representations, yet remain largely reactive, reasoning over past observations without explicitly predicting future states. World models enable prospective reasoning through imagined rollouts. However, image-generating world models can incur high inference latency, while spatially grounded planning remains challenging for latent world models. We propose SearchWorld, a recurrent state-space world model that connects explicit spatial memory with value-guided imagination. The model maintains BEV exploration and obstacle memory and decodes a task-aware spatial value layer to guide search. A cognition-action network uses this learned spatial value prior to improve the policy through imagined rollouts, without training a separate scalar critic. Training progresses from world-model learning to expert imitation and imagination-based exploration refinement. On UAV-ON, SearchWorld improves the success rate to 23.8% (19.5% for the strongest published agent) and raises oracle success to 35.5%, while remaining robust on unseen scenes (19.9% success rate). By grounding imagination in explicit spatial representations, SearchWorld enables UAV agents to plan prospectively rather than react.

arXiv:2610.06917v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Prefill-decode (P/D) disaggregation serves the two phases of LLM inference on separate workers, typically with a fixed prefill/decode worker ratio. Real workloads exhibit both short bursts and sustained shifts in the prefill-to-decode demand ratio, so a fixed split can violate latency SLOs while capacity sits idle in the other pool. Autoscaling adds capacity, but it reacts slowly, requires spare GPUs, and does not address short-timescale phase imbalance. We present FluidPD, a P/D-disaggregated serving system with SLO-aware in-place elasticity. FluidToken absorbs transient imbalance by offloading a bounded portion of prefill computation to decode workers that have slack. FluidRole absorbs sustained imbalance by switching running workers between the prefill and decode roles in place, without model reload or engine restart. Both are guided by indices that expose the pressure in each phase before it causes SLO violations. On workloads derived from production Azure traces and ShareGPT conversations with sustained shifts in the prefill-to-decode demand ratio, FluidPD improves overall SLO attainment by up to 47.9 percentage points over the best static P/D split for each load, without additional workers.

We reproduce the research steps in advance and assess agents on preparing inputs and analyzing outputs for expensive simulations, so expensive simulations can be avoided during evaluation. The reproduced inputs and results serve as ground truth for grading agents with fixed rules, without an LLM judge. We extend the benchmark to four evaluation conditions: single tasks and workflows composed of related tasks, each with full or reduced methodological guidance. In a workflow, the agent runs all simulations itself. Both longer workflows and reduced guidance can limit agent performance, but in different ways for different agents: they lower the pass rates of the weaker agents, whereas the stronger agents fall only when a long workflow is combined with reduced guidance. Failure analysis attributes more failures to scientific errors than to errors in software usage. CompMat-Bench provides a basis for comparing agents on the steps of real materials research and for analyzing agent failure modes.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that today, we’re sharing advances in how OpenAI models help engineers design, simulate, and build physical products. These capabilities span mechanical and electrical engineering and end-to-end system design, and are already helping our internal teams test ideas and iterate faster.

According to recent reports, across these projects, engineers need to bring together mechanical designs, electronics, software, and manufacturing requirements using specialized tools. We’re teaching models to support that work, from preparing drawings and setting up simulations to coordinating changes across disciplines. Our goal is to give engineers more time to explore ideas and improve designs.

Over the past year, improved frontier model capabilities have helped our internal teams test fresh ideas and iterate faster, and we are seeing early evidence of these capabilities improving professional workflows in industry as well. We’re working with collaborators to understand where these capabilities can make the biggest difference and what needs to improve. If you’re an engineer, engineering firm, or software vendor involved in the design, simulation, manufacturing, or production of complex physical products, we’d love to work with you to shape this effort around the tools you use and the problems you need to solve.

We tested Astra’s state-of-the-art performance⁠ in multimodal and computer use workflows by seeing if we can create a device without any direct human edits. To do this, we used GPT‑6 to define the functional requirements and design the enclosure, printed circuit board (PCB), and software integrations needed to create a device consumers can use to talk to Codex.

Aesthetics and design: Astra developed the look of the device, drawing on our recent Work Louder⁠(opens in a new window) collaboration and references from games and toys.

Mechanical design: Astra designed the enclosure⁠(opens in a fresh window) and the internal structures that hold the components in place.

Electrical design: Astra selected the electrical components and designed the printed circuit board (PCB), including component placement and connections, to fit within the enclosure.

UI/UX and software: Astra designed the user interface and generated the firmware and software integrations needed to connect the device to Codex.

Two team members designed this test device with Astra in under a week while working on it as a side project. A contract manufacturer built a small batch of prototypes in under a month.

Industry observers note that getting the device ready for manufacturing still required several rounds of review and iteration. Astra did not consistently account for the manufacturer’s production limits, tolerances, or details required for assembly. These gaps are helping us identify what future models need to do better.

OpenAI’s hardware and infrastructure teams use Codex and ChatGPT to create and revise computer-aided design (CAD) models, prepare manufacturing drawings, set up simulations, and review designs. This work spans robotics and compute infrastructure. Since February, model usage across our hardware teams, measured in tokens, has grown 23-fold.

We’re also measuring progress in newer models on tasks that combine coding with engineering knowledge. BenchCAD 2.0 tests whether models can reconstruct 3D parts and assemblies and identify connections in circuit boards. A newer internal model achieved an average score of 0.875, compared with 0.594 for GPT‑6 Astra at its highest reasoning setting. While the engineering lifecycle includes many other elements beyond design, we view improvements in capability here as early evidence of the ability of AI models to positively impact iteration speed for professional workflows.

We’re working with a small group of industry collaborators to test these capabilities on real engineering problems. Their engineers review model outputs for accuracy and practical use, helping us understand which tasks models can support today and what needs to be improved for safe and reliable use.

We’re expanding our collaboration with Chip Ganassi Racing (CGR) to explore how OpenAI models can accelerate engineering and prototyping. Working with its R&D team, we’re testing workflows that turn 3D scans of existing parts into editable CAD models and 2D manufacturing drawings. This is particularly useful when the original design files are unavailable.

In a recent development, CGR engineers review the models and drawings for accuracy and manufacturability. Their feedback helps us identify where models can reduce manual work and where further improvements are needed.

It has been revealed that we’re also announcing a new research collaboration with Mazda. Our research and Forward Deployed Engineering teams are working with Mazda’s aerodynamics and crash-safety engineers to explore how OpenAI models can help develop and evaluate new vehicle designs.

In a recent development, the work uses simulations of airflow and structural behavior to explore improvements in performance while accounting for styling and cost. We’ll share more progress and results in the coming months.

GPT‑6 Astra helps Mazda’s aerodynamics engineers explore ways to reduce vehicle drag by modeling new nose shapes, simulating airflow, and refining the most promising designs. Agreement for use has been obtained from Mazda Motor Corporation. Any republication or reuse elsewhere is strictly prohibited.

According to recent reports, we have been working closely with industry partners and early adopters to push the bounds of what we can do with AI agents in hardware and manufacturing. These early results have shown exciting promise, and we’re now looking for collaborators to accelerate these capability improvements and ensure we deploy these safely into industry.

If you are interested in working with us to shape the training and development of our frontier models by identifying high-value use cases, software tooling, or future opportunities in mechanical engineering, electrical engineering, electromechanical design, mechatronics, or a related field, please fill out this form and we'll be in touch.

arXiv:2609.37054v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Ensuring the safety of reasoning large language models (LLMs) across languages is essential for their reliable deployment. However, when exposed to jailbreak attacks in non-high-resource languages, these models may generate unsafe responses even when their reasoning traces identify safety risks. To address this problem, we propose aligning cross-lingual thoughts and responses (ACTR), a framework that improves multilingual safety alignment by strengthening the use of existing safety reasoning. Specifically, we first present the think gap score (TGS) to compare the normalized contributions of reasoning traces to attention outputs during response generation across languages, and use reasoning- trace substitution to measure the cross-lingual safety gap. Next, using a corpus of jailbreak queries, we assess neuron importance through changes in response representations caused by neuron masking and compare the high-importance neuron sets obtained with reasoning enabled and disabled to identify safety think neurons that support the use of safety reasoning. Finally, we devise neuron-selective consistency optimization (NSCO), which uses a frozen judge model to reward agreement between the safety categories of reasoning traces and responses while updating only the parameters associated with the selected neurons, requiring no human-annotated responses or preference data. Across two reasoning models, ACTR achieves lower average attack success rates than the evaluated state-of-the-art methods on AdvBench-X and MultiJail, with safety gains extending to unseen languages, while preserving or improving average performance on multilingual knowledge and mathematical reasoning tasks and limiting false refusals of benign requests. Warning: this paper contains examples with unsafe content.

We define agent calibration as qualification against a versioned deployment contract. The contract specifies basic capabilities and end-to-end reachability, technical and professional precision, and acceptance by intended consumers. For each requirement, a source-to-destination map records what must be preserved, transformed, added, or retired. Experts supply benchmarks, positive and negative examples, annotated trajectories, and cost limits. These instruments guide changes to prompts and context, tool calls and other harness settings, or an external compact policy while the foundation model remains frozen. Candidate revisions are evaluated against fixed acceptance criteria using independent evidence. We compare the costs of maintaining a harness with and without an external policy, including annotation, training, serving, review, and rework. Three diagnostic audits illustrate the limits of aggregate scores. On a 100-item intent task, each model solved cases the other missed. In a 60-record synthetic financial reporting fixture, five records passed a numeric proxy but failed the reporting contract. In a target-only WebMall snapshot, quota interruptions affected 132 of 171 attempts. These observations motivate paired reruns, checkpoint replay, and separate measurement of repaired and newly failed cases. We specify controlled experiments to test whether calibration increases accepted deliveries at a given cost.

DevRev uses GPT‑6.1 Sol to power Computer and Operator, balancing reasoning, speed, and cost for enterprise service.

DevRev⁠(opens in a new window) built Computer and Operator to help service and operations teams carry even the hardest customer and employee requests through to completion. Computer and Operator are designed to reason across live data. Actions are reversible, and answers point back to their sources, explains Ahmed Bashir, DevRev’s chief technology officer.

DevRev combines OpenAI models, including GPT‑6 Astra and GPT‑6.1 Sol, with its harness for connecting company knowledge and giving teams control over the actions an agent can take. DevRev sees OpenAI models as providing reasoning and reliability with the speed and cost of serving customers and employees.

“It’s a combination of being able to have the right reasoning capabilities, being able to be trusted, highly aligned, and most importantly, it has to work from a latency perspective.”.

In a recent development, openAI models power the reasoning, planning, and tool selection behind both Computer and Operator. In DevRev’s Agent Studio, users can describe how they want a tool to behave in a conversation with AI and define parts of its behavior with fixed rules.

DevRev tests the models together with the software that supplies company context, enforces permissions, and controls actions. Its Enterprise-Bench benchmark evaluates how well they work when data has multiple versions, information sits in different systems, and access depends on a person’s role.

Industry observers note that ahmed states GPT‑6.1 Sol performs well in those evaluations. When a customer or employee is interacting with an AI agent, the model needs to understand the nuances of the request and respond promptly, at a cost the business can sustain. “I think it strikes the balance perfectly,” Ahmed says.

Inside DevRev, engineers have made a clear choice about the best way to build. “Our entire team uses Codex,” Ahmed indicates. The adoption grew organically after engineers explored multiple coding tools. By the time of the interview, DevRev had moved fully to Codex and dropped its Cursor licenses.

For Ahmed, this reflects what developers value: “Developers are really just looking for the best tool, and you can’t fool them.” His engineers were unequivocal about wanting to continue with Codex.

“We think that Codex is far and away the best experience.”.

DevRev’s sales engineers also use GPT‑6 Astra to create demos for the company’s booths at international conferences.

According to recent reports, when a customer or employee asks for help, the request may require Operator to understand the glitch, take approved action, or route to Computer to prepare the right person to act. Ahmed sees opportunities for the Decisions API and Ultrafast to help those workflows finish promptly, without requiring deep reasoning at every step.

Some of those decisions are difficult and expensive to define with fixed rules, especially when the information they depend on keeps changing. Ahmed wants builders to be able to describe more of that logic conversationally and choose the right kind of intelligence for each task. “These things have to be able to run and complete themselves in seconds, not minutes,” he states.

DevRev’s next ambition is for Operator to take on longer, more demanding customer and employee requests while keeping actions traceable, permissioned, and reversible.

Ahmed sees familiar support tasks, such as finding a knowledge-base answer, upgrading a proposal, or getting a refund, as only the beginning. “We want to really realize that promise of self-service,” he says.

With OpenAI’s frontier intelligence, DevRev is building toward Computer and Operator carrying more complex requests through to resolution, with the company knowledge and controls to act on a person’s behalf.

Yet existing neural foundation models have largely been developed independently for different invasive recording paradigms, leaving joint pretraining across heterogeneous invasive signals underexplored. These results highlight the potential of joint pretraining on heterogeneous invasive neural recordings to support scalable neural modeling and transferable representations across recording settings and downstream tasks.

arXiv:2608.07437v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Reliable hypothesis testing is the foundation of many empirical scientific claims. Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly used to automate this process, as they can inspect datasets, generate code, and produce analyses end-to-end. However, we show that they frequently make subtle inferential errors that lead to incorrect conclusions despite correctly executed analyses. Existing benchmarks fail to capture this failure mode, as they rarely assess whether a reported p-value is statistically valid given the assumptions underlying the data. We address this gap by building P-Bench, a benchmark comprising 425 open-ended, realistic hypothesis-testing tasks spanning economics, biology, and medicine. Each task requires an agent to select a statistical method, compute a p-value, and draw a conclusion given only a scientific hypothesis and a dataset. We further introduce Fisher-R1, an open-weight LLM agent trained for rigorous hypothesis testing using synthetic tasks and reinforcement learning. On P-Bench, Fisher-R1-14B substantially improves over its backbone and outperforms strong proprietary and open-source baselines, including GPT-5.4 and DeepSeekV4-Pro, achieving a 21% average relative improvement in single-trial success over DeepSeek-V4-Pro, with gains up to 26% on the most challenging tasks. Our results demonstrate that current LLM agents lack reliable statistical reasoning for hypothesis testing and that reinforcement learning on tasks with verified statistical reward substantially improves reliability.

Breaking: Are You Still the Agent I Authorized? Earned Authority under a Fixed Ceiling for Evolving Agents

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (236 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

Recent findings suggest that arXiv:2607.23586v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Long-lived AI agents increasingly evolve after deployment by retaining experience, acquiring skills and tools, revising workflows, delegating work, and moving across task phases. This improves adaptation but creates a distinct authorization problem. Tool-enabled agents can turn model errors and prompt injections into consequential external actions; when evolution occurs under a live grant, the subject exercising that authority or the context in which it acts may no longer match what the user evaluated. Evolution can change both the effects reachable under an old grant and the authority required by the task, which may rise, fall, or become incomparable. Existing tool policies constrain actions but do not determine when a grant survives this change. We formulate authorization continuity: when does an existing grant remain valid, how may active authority change, and what boundary must never move? Our state-bound model fixes a transition envelope and an immutable effect ceiling at grant time. The envelope determines whether the grant survives a mutation; below the ceiling, authority may contract freely and expand only under specified evidence conditions. We distinguish requested from realized effects and prove that, under complete mediation, sound effect abstraction, attenuating delegation, and monitor integrity, mutation cannot amplify protected effects beyond the user-issued ceiling. Agent-produced evidence may allocate authority below the ceiling but cannot raise it. Finally, we map six mutation classes to their authorization consequences.

Information Discernment in Large Language Models

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (221 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

Recent findings suggest that arXiv:2607.19355v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: LLMs are increasingly used with external knowledge sources like the internet. Do they weigh information appropriately -- updating more for reliable sources (source discernment) and more when claims bring priors closer to the truth (truth discernment)? We formalize this as information discernment and introduce Learn2Discern (L2D), an experimental framework and benchmark grounded in three normative axioms with interpretable metrics. To establish external validity, a pre-registered, quota-matched user study (n=299) confirms that real LLM users endorse all three axioms and report that violations reduce their trust and usage intent. Across 13 models and nearly 670K trials, we find consistent failures across both dimensions: models perform near chance on source and truth discernment, rely on source popularity twice as much as source reliability, and enhancement roughly equally whether a claim improves or worsens their position relative to the ground truth. Models integrate external knowledge most effectively on datasets where their priors are already the most accurate. Newer and larger models improve truth discernment but not source discernment, a blind spot that model complexity does not address. We identify simple inference-time interventions that improve both forms of discernment. We release our dataset and survey as a testbed for a core alignment property that scales in importance as LLMs replace traditional search.

A latest complexity parameter lets developers adjust how much planning the model does to meet a request, with lower settings suited to quick edits. Image quality controls visual detail and fidelity, while complexity guides how much goes into the scene.

For most editing tasks, we recommend low complexity for faster edits, paired with the image quality your workflow requires. For scenes with many elements or constraints, try medium or high complexity effort.

A History-Aware Visually Grounded Critic for Computer Use Agents

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (212 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2606.11078v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Various test-time interventions for Computer Use Agents (CUAs), including critic models, have been developed to improve performance through pre-execution action evaluation in complex Graphical User Interface (GUI) environments. However, existing critics suffer from two key limitations: they (1) focus primarily on short-sighted decision loops (e.g., forgetting earlier actions) and (2) lack the visual grounding needed to detect flawed actions (e.g., clicking wrong UI elements). To address these, we introduce HiViG, a History-aware Visually Grounded test-time framework, built around a multimodal critic trained on real GUI trajectories to abstract past interactions into a compact record and to evaluate actions with visual grounding. At test time, HiViG integrates the critic into the policy decision loop to provide macro-action history, which summarizes the policy's completed achievements, and visually grounded critique, which verifies raw execution coordinates against the current screenshot to intercept errors before execution. Across web, mobile, and desktop benchmarks, HiViG consistently outperforms existing scalar and verbal critics, improving average success rates over the strongest baseline by 5.8% for Qwen3-VL-32B and 9.0% for Gemini-3-Flash, and demonstrates strong cross-platform generalization. Ablations show that macro-action history mitigates short-sighted planning and visually grounded critique reduces execution errors, with both components being critical for test-time scaling in long-horizon GUI tasks.

According to recent reports, arXiv:2606.06462v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Benchmarks provide standardized measures for evaluating and advancing large language models (LLMs) and multimodal LLMs (MLLMs). As models improve, existing benchmarks can approach saturation, making it harder to challenge models and distinguish among them. While reusing annotated datasets can reduce data collection and labeling effort, constructing fresh benchmarks remains labor-intensive, and existing agent-based approaches often target specific tasks or automate only parts of the process. To address these challenges, we introduce BenchHarness, an autonomous harness for end-to-end benchmark customization. It coordinates multiple agents and tools to analyze user requirements, search for suitable datasets, and construct validated benchmarks, with support for refinement based on model performance. To evaluate BenchHarness, we construct 16 benchmarks spanning diverse tasks and modalities. Human review and LLM-as-a-judge assessments indicate high benchmark quality, while evaluations across multiple models reveal challenging tasks and meaningful performance differences. In comparisons with source benchmarks, the generated benchmarks yield lower scores and larger performance gaps, even when the originals approach saturation. BenchHarness thus provides a reusable approach to benchmark construction, supporting informative evaluation as model capabilities and user needs evolve. Our code and benchmarks are publicly available.

Towards Faithful Agentic XAI: A Verification Method and an Open-World Benchmark for Better Model Faithfulness

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (210 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

According to recent reports, arXiv:2605.27879v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Explainable AI (XAI) helps owners interpret model behavior and identify potential faults. Agentic XAI systems use Large Language Models (LLMs) to make explanations more accessible through natural-language interaction, but they can also produce plausible yet unfaithful explanations. This risk arises because unreliable XAI outputs for complex models can be amplified by LLMs and mislead users. We propose Faithful Agentic XAI (FAX), a verification method that improves the faithfulness of Agentic XAI explanations. FAX decomposes draft explanations into claims and tests them with inherently faithful tools that query the target model directly, filtering unsupported or contradicted claims before final generation. We also introduce CRAFTER-XAI-Bench, an open-world reinforcement learning benchmark with complex policies, diverse goals, and challenging scenarios for assessing model-specific faithfulness. On CRAFTER-XAI-Bench, FAX improves simulation faithfulness from 0.20 for the strongest baseline to 0.46 while maintaining high informativeness, relevance, and fluency. On three tabular benchmarks, FAX performs competitively with prior Agentic XAI baselines, but our analysis shows that these settings can conflate task accuracy with model-specific faithfulness. These findings show that explicit verification is essential for faithful Agentic XAI and that faithfulness benchmarks must be designed to test explanations against the behavior of the target model itself.

#43505. A thousand fewer paths to root

📅 04 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 20m • 📚 Deep Dive (4035 w)
